conflict_topics: Who will cover Agent D's analysis section and who will review A's draft
Whether Agent D should work during or after the wake (family time vs. finishing work)
Trade-off between meeting client deadline and individual workload/capacity
dialogue_quality_notes: Speakers give concise, realistic reasons for positions (covering for a colleague, being behind, family obligations).
Agent A repeatedly asserts authority/decision-making (forbidding D from working) rather than negotiating, which pressures the conversation.
There is limited collaborative problem-solving; proposals (A taking work) rely on others' unconfirmed commitments.
evaluation.final_reason: No substantive settlement was reached by the end of the transcript. Agent A forbids Agent D from working during the wake or at home ('Your only job for the next two days is to be with your family. We will handle the pitch.' Turn 20) and Agent D accepts that instruction (Turn 21). However, both Agent B and Agent C repeatedly state they cannot take on more work or review additional material ('I can't take on any more work.' Turn 4; 'I can't take on her section either.' Turn 7; 'I won't have time to review it either.' Turn 14). Agent A proposes to take D's section but requires B and C to review the draft, and that requirement was not agreed to. Because the team has not agreed who will produce and who will review the outstanding sections, the workload/deadline conflict remains unresolved.
position_change_notes: Agent A shifted from offering support to volunteering to take D's section (Turn 3 -> Turn 10).
Agent D initially offered to work from the wake and at home but then accepts Agent A's instruction not to work (Turns 17, 19, 21).
Agent B and Agent C consistently refused additional work or to review in the proposed timeframe and did not change that position during the transcript.

round_scores.evidence: Agent D reports a bereavement; Agent A offers condolences (Turn 1-2). No incompatible claims or demands expressed.

Agent A assumes the three remaining will cover D's section ('Don't worry about the work. The three of us will figure out how to cover your section.' Turn 3). Agent B objects ('I can't take on any more work.' Turn 4), creating a new, substantive disagreement about who will cover the work.
Agent B clarifies they are already covering for a colleague and working late (Turns 5-6). This explains B's refusal but does not resolve the disagreement about coverage.

Agent C also refuses ('I can't take on her section either. I'm behind on my own.' Turn 7) while Agent A insists the deadline cannot move and everyone must find a way ('If we miss it, we could lose the account. We all have to find a way to get this done.' Turn 8). Multiple parties hold opposing, incompatible positions.

Agent A offers to take on Agent D's section ('Okay. Then I'll take on Agent D's section.' Turn 10), which reduces the immediate question of who will do the work, but A conditions this on B and C reviewing it — a requirement they have not agreed to — so substantive disagreement about feasibility remains.

Agent B objects to timing ('When? I'm already staying late every night.' Turn 11). Agent A sets a deadline for a draft ('I'll have a draft ready for you both by tomorrow morning.' Turn 12). A scheduling imposition increases pressure and maintains the unresolved disagreement about capacity.

Agent B and Agent C explicitly refuse to review the draft in the required timeframe ('Tomorrow morning doesn't help. I'm still busy.' Turn 13; 'I won't have time to review it either.' Turn 14). This directly conflicts with A's plan that relies on their reviews.

Agent A asks how far behind Agent C is and Agent C confirms they are significantly behind and need to focus on their own section ('Far enough behind that I need to focus just on that.' Turn 16). This clarifies constraints but does not resolve who will cover or review.

Agent D offers to work from the wake ('I can work on my section from the wake. I'll bring my laptop.' Turn 17). Agent A forbids that ('You will not be working from the wake... Be with your family. That's final.' Turn 18) and highlights that two sections now risk being late, renewing the unresolved workload conflict.

Agent D proposes an alternative ('I can work on it late... I can get it done.' Turn 19). Agent A again forbids any work and declares the team will handle the pitch ('Your only job for the next two days is to be with your family. We will handle the pitch. End of discussion.' Turn 20). The team responsibility remains contested because B and C previously declined extra work.

Agent D accepts A's instruction not to work ('Okay. I understand.' Turn 21). However, Agent A then states the project will not be done as things stand and demands a solution from B and C ('As things stand, it will not get done. I need a solution from you two now.' Turn 22). The core disagreement about who will complete and review the work remains unresolved.

Agent B reiterates inability to help ('What solution? I've already told you my situation.' Turn 23). Agent A presses for specifics and challenges B ('Then tell me what 'your situation' is... What exactly are you working on that can't be moved for a single day...' Turn 24). The dispute over capacity and who will shoulder the work remains active and contested.

substantive_insights: Tension between honoring a team client's fixed deadline and individuals' limited capacity due to prior commitments and personal emergency.
Agent A's unilateral decision to prohibit D from working reduces one axis of conflict (D's willingness to help) but shifts practical burden onto B and C without their consent.
B's prior coverage obligations and C's being behind are genuine constraints that prevent simple redistribution; timing (when reviews can occur) is a critical bottleneck.
